design_detail: Inpatient human laboratory study (short report), within-person: six people who smoked cocaine almost daily each completed eight sessions. In the first four sessions the alternative to cocaine was a voucher for $5 in money, in the last four a $5 merchandise voucher (fixed order, not randomized or counterbalanced); each session offered one cocaine dose level (0 mg placebo, 12, 25 or 50 mg smoked cocaine base; order of doses within each block not reported). A session began with a sample trial (the session's dose and its voucher type), followed by five choice trials 14 minutes apart, each requiring 200 key presses for the chosen option. Outcome: number of cocaine choices (0–5 per session, 0–20 per voucher type). Described by the authors as double-blind.
can_establish: That in six people who smoked cocaine almost daily, studied as inpatients, cocaine choices rose with dose, and that about two fewer of 20 cocaine options were taken when a $5 money voucher was the alternative than when a $5 merchandise voucher was, under this fixed-order procedure.
cannot_establish: Whether money itself rather than the order of the conditions (money sessions always came first) produced the difference; how much either voucher reduced cocaine choice (there was no condition without an alternative); whether the difference holds at any single dose (none was significant), in people seeking treatment, outside the laboratory, or for abstinence (not measured).

sample.recruitment: Word-of-mouth referral and newspaper advertisements in New York City; inpatients of the Irving Center for Clinical Research, New York Presbyterian Hospital, for the whole study, with television, radio and films available and visitors not allowed (p. 88, Methods › Participants; Procedure, 1st paragraph). Whether participants were seeking treatment is not stated.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Almost daily use of smoked cocaine; passing comprehensive medical and psychological evaluations; serum pregnancy test at screening and urine pregnancy test at the start of sessions for women (p. 88). No diagnostic criteria and no criteria about other drug use are reported.
sample.demographics: Four women (three African-American, one Hispanic) and two men (both Caucasian); age 30–39 years (mean 36); spending $100–$500 (mean $280) a week on cocaine (p. 88).
sample.attrition: None reported; Figure 2 shows all six participants in both voucher conditions (p. 89).
sample.selection_effects: A small self-selected group of people who smoked cocaine frequently and consented to an inpatient study in which cocaine would be given, possibly daily (p. 88); not described as treatment-seeking. The authors report that all participants used substantially larger amounts of cocaine outside the laboratory than in the sessions (p. 90).

exposure.measurement: Cocaine given by research staff in each session; choices recorded by computer (pp. 88–89).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: smoked cocaine base, prepared by the hospital pharmacy from cocaine hydrochloride supplied by the National Institute on Drug Abuse, at 0 (placebo), 12, 25 or 50 mg per dose; one dose level per session, a sample dose plus up to five chosen doses at 14-minute intervals, each given only if heart rate and blood pressure were within the study's preset safety limits (pp. 88–89). The number of sessions per day and the interval between sessions are not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco cigarettes were allowed outside sessions (p. 88); alcohol and other drug use are not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Inpatient throughout; time since last cocaine use before the first session and any urine toxicology are not reported.

comparison.controls: Within-person: each participant's choices with a $5 money voucher against a $5 merchandise voucher (redeemable at specific stores), across the same four dose levels; 0 mg served as a placebo dose. No condition without an alternative (p. 90, Discussion, 3rd paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a within-person comparison; how much each participant valued money relative to merchandise was not measured.

outcomes.instruments: Number of cocaine choices per session (0–5) and per voucher type (0–20), recorded by computer. Subjective-effects questionnaires, heart rate and blood pressure every 2 minutes, and blood samples were also collected (p. 88, Apparatus), but no results for them are reported.
outcomes.validity_norms: The choice procedure and the merchandise vouchers are the laboratory's own, used in its studies of possible cocaine medications (Haney et al. 1998, 1999; Ward et al. 1998, as cited, pp. 87, 90).
outcomes.operationalization: Reinforcing effect of cocaine = number of times the cocaine option was chosen over the voucher; effectiveness of an alternative = fewer cocaine choices. The 0 mg (placebo) choices are counted as cocaine choices.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None reported: one two-factor repeated-measures ANOVA (dose × voucher type) plus voucher comparisons at each of the four doses (p. 89).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Choices were recorded automatically. The design is called double-blind (p. 87), but each sample trial told participants which voucher was available (p. 88); participants closed their eyes when given a dose to hide dose cues; how staff were blinded is not described.

analysis.effect_sizes: Dose: F(3, 15)=15.26, P<0.001; voucher type: F(1, 5)=7.48, P<0.05; no significant interaction and no significant voucher difference at any single dose (p. 89, Results). Editors' reading of Figure 2 at 300 dpi (bar heights fall on whole numbers): total cocaine choices out of 20, money vs merchandise, 15 vs 16, 7 vs 7, 12 vs 14, 12 vs 16, 2 vs 7 and 16 vs 17; means 10.7 vs 12.8. Editors' calculation: mean paired difference 2.17 choices (95% CI 0.13 to 4.20; dz 1.12); the paired t of 2.73 squares to 7.48, reproducing the printed F(1, 5). Editors' reading of Figure 1 (means fall on sixths): money vs merchandise, 0 mg 0.67 vs 1.50, 12 mg 2.50 vs 2.67, 25 mg 3.67 vs 4.17, 50 mg 3.83 vs 4.50 choices of 5; 0.83 of the 2.17 difference (38%) came from the placebo sessions (placebo chosen on 4 vs 9 of 30 trials), and for the active doses the totals were 60 vs 68 of 90 choices.
analysis.selective_reporting: Subjective-effects ratings, heart rate, blood pressure and blood samples were collected (p. 88) but not reported; the order of doses within each voucher block is not reported.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Six inpatients chose cocaine more often as the dose rose, and on average 2.2 fewer of 20 cocaine options (95% CI 0.1 to 4.2, editors' calculation) in the money-voucher sessions, which always came first, than in the merchandise-voucher sessions; no single dose showed a significant difference, one participant chose identically in both, and more than a third of the difference came from placebo sessions.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the data demonstrate that money vouchers are a more effective alternative reinforcer than merchandise vouchers, generalizing to people who use cocaine (p. 87). The discussion turns the difference into money being 10% more effective and suggests a $5.50 merchandise voucher would in theory equal $5.00 in cash (p. 90), a proportionality not tested; it concedes that there was no condition without a voucher and no randomization of order, and argues order effects are unlikely from the group's other studies and participants' reports of heavier use outside (p. 90). It then extends the result to outpatient contingency management, suggesting cash or larger vouchers would further enhance abstinence (p. 90), an outcome not measured here.

timeline.event: Higgins, Bickel & Hughes: in a laboratory study, intranasal cocaine choice fell as the value of a money alternative rose (as described, p. 87).
Hatsukami et al.: smoked cocaine self-administration fell as money value rose (as described, p. 90).
Chutuape et al.: methadone patients rewarded for drug-free urine chose cash vouchers over a take-home dose 75% of the time (as described, p. 90).
This study: money vs merchandise vouchers of equal face value, six inpatients, fixed order.

replication.where_it_stands: No replication of the money-versus-merchandise comparison is among the papers read for this round. The earlier laboratory studies the authors cite found that larger money alternatives reduced cocaine choice; the field evidence that non-drug alternatives reduce use comes from contingency management trials, not from this study.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse grant DA-06234; the Irving Center for Clinical Research of the New York Presbyterian Medical Center, where participants resided, supported by National Institutes of Health grant MOI-RR-00645 (Acknowledgements, p. 91).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Division on Substance Abuse, New York State Psychiatric Institute, and Department of Psychiatry, College of Physicians and Surgeons of Columbia University (p. 87). Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A within-person study with randomized or counterbalanced order of alternatives, a condition without any alternative, several values of each kind of voucher, analyses of active doses separately from placebo, and enough participants (including people seeking treatment); then a field comparison of cash and merchandise incentives in contingency management with abstinence as the outcome.

domains.note: Money-voucher sessions always came first and merchandise sessions last; the order of doses within each block is not reported.

The voucher comparison coincides completely with period (sessions 1–4 against 5–8), so changes over the stay (tolerance, habituation to the unit, accumulating vouchers) cannot be separated from voucher type; the authors' argument against order effects rests on other studies and self-report.

Participants knew the voucher type by design (unavoidable for this question); called double-blind without describing staff blinding; doses could be withheld under the vital-sign limits, and whether any were is not reported.
All six participants completed both voucher conditions (Figure 2).
No protocol; subjective, cardiovascular and blood measures were collected but not reported; the per-dose comparisons are reported as not significant, but without statistics.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: RoB 2 applied to the within-person comparison of money and merchandise vouchers (the dose–response finding is less exposed). Because the two voucher conditions ran in a fixed order, the voucher effect cannot be separated from time in the study; with six participants it rests on one F test at P<0.05, and no single dose showed a difference. The outcome was recorded automatically and no one dropped out. Cite the paper as a small laboratory demonstration that the kind of non-drug alternative offered can shift cocaine choices in people who smoke cocaine frequently, with the fixed order and the size of the difference (about 2 of 20 choices, a third of it from placebo sessions) stated; do not cite it for treatment, abstinence, or a general ranking of cash over goods.

key_findings.finding: Six people took part: four women (three African-American, one Hispanic) and two Caucasian men, aged 30–39 (mean 36), recruited by word of mouth and newspaper advertisements in New York City; all reported almost daily smoked cocaine use and spending $100–$500 (mean $280) a week on cocaine, and all passed medical and psychological evaluations. Whether they were seeking treatment is not stated.

Participants lived on an inpatient research unit for the whole study and completed eight sessions: four with a $5 money voucher as the alternative, then four with a $5 merchandise voucher; each session offered one dose level (0, 12, 25 or 50 mg smoked cocaine) in a sample trial and five choice trials 14 minutes apart, each choice requiring 200 key presses, with doses given only within preset heart-rate and blood-pressure limits; tobacco smoking was allowed between sessions.

Cocaine choices increased with dose (F(3, 15)=15.26, P<0.001) and were fewer when the money voucher was the alternative (F(1, 5)=7.48, P<0.05); there was no significant interaction, and no significant difference between voucher types at any single dose (0, 12, 25 or 50 mg).
All but one participant chose more cocaine doses in the merchandise sessions than in the money sessions (maximum 20 per condition).
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of Figure 2 at 300 dpi (bar heights fall on whole numbers): money vs merchandise 15 vs 16, 7 vs 7, 12 vs 14, 12 vs 16, 2 vs 7 and 16 vs 17; means 10.7 vs 12.8. Editors' calculation: mean paired difference 2.17 (95% CI 0.13 to 4.20; dz 1.12); the paired t (2.73) squares to the printed F(1, 5) of 7.48.

key_findings.finding: Figure 1 shows mean cocaine choices (of 5) by dose and voucher type, rising with dose in both conditions, with the merchandise line above the money line at every dose and the largest gap at 0 mg.
key_findings.note: Editors' reading at 300 dpi (means fall on sixths, consistent with the totals in Figure 2): money vs merchandise 0.67 vs 1.50 at 0 mg, 2.50 vs 2.67 at 12 mg, 3.67 vs 4.17 at 25 mg, 3.83 vs 4.50 at 50 mg. Editors' calculation: 0.83 of the 2.17 difference (38%) came from placebo sessions (placebo chosen on 4 vs 9 of 30 trials); active doses 60 vs 68 of 90 choices.

key_findings.finding: The authors express the result as about two fewer of 20 doses with money vouchers, call money vouchers 10% more effective, and suggest that raising merchandise value by 10% ($5.50 against $5.00 in cash) would in theory make the two equivalent. They acknowledge that without a no-voucher condition the absolute influence of either voucher cannot be quantified, and that the order was not randomized (cash first), but judge order effects unlikely because participants in their studies change little across sessions and reported using substantially larger amounts outside the laboratory.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (left column, continuing in the right column)

key_findings.finding: The laboratory had used merchandise vouchers in its medication studies to lower the chance that participants would buy drugs with their earnings after discharge; the authors suggest that money alternatives could make laboratory tests of possible cocaine medications more sensitive.

The authors extend the result to outpatient treatment: cash or merchandise vouchers of greater value would further enhance abstinence; in support they cite a contingency-management study in which methadone patients chose cash vouchers over a methadone take-home dose 75% of the time.

Subjective-effects questionnaires were completed, heart rate and blood pressure were recorded every 2 minutes from 30 minutes before dosing, and a catheter was placed for blood withdrawals, but only choice data are reported.

reporting_issues.issue: The study is called double-blind, but each session's sample trial gave participants a voucher showing which alternative was available, so the voucher comparison was open by design; how staff were blinded is not described.
reporting_issues.consequence: At most the dose could have been blinded; expectations about the vouchers could act on choices.

reporting_issues.issue: The counted cocaine choices include choices of the 0 mg (placebo) dose; by the editors' reading of Figure 1, 38% of the voucher difference came from placebo sessions, and for the active doses the totals were 60 vs 68 of 90 choices.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's statement that significantly less cocaine was self-administered with money vouchers overstates the effect on active cocaine; the difference on active doses was about 1.3 of 15 choices.

reporting_issues.issue: The Figure 2 legend refers to asterisks marking significant differences between voucher conditions, but only the group means carry one; the error bars on the means are not defined, and their length matches the SD of the six totals (editors' calculation: 5.3 and 4.6), whereas Figure 1's bars are SEM.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; individual participants' differences were not tested, and readers could take Figure 2's bars for SEM.

reporting_issues.issue: Subjective-effects ratings, heart rate, blood pressure and blood samples were collected but not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Selective reporting cannot be ruled out, and whether any dose was withheld under the vital-sign limits is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: The order of dose levels within each voucher block, the number of sessions per day and the interval between sessions are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The dose comparison could also be confounded with order or time, and the schedule cannot be compared with real-world use.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), pp. 87–91: all pages read on rendered pages at 150 dpi; Figures 1 and 2 enlarged at 300 dpi and read against the axis ticks (Figure 2 bar heights fall on whole numbers and reproduce the printed F(1, 5) by paired t); no supplement.
